title: Gateless Barrier, Case 5: Hsiang-yen: Up a Tree
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 5 of the Mumonkan, Xiang Yan's story of a man hanging from a tree by his teeth, who must answer a question about Bodhidharma or lose his life. Opening with a Gary Snyder poem about log truck drivers and a Wendell Berry poem, "The Real Work," Nomon links the koan to the practice period's study of maturity and to the upcoming shuso ceremony. Yamada Kuan's commentary calls for a response that is "factual," and Nyogen Senzaki calls the story a "kindness of unkind action." Nomon closes with Norman's advice to be humble, see everyone as Buddha, and try to help, then sings a Cat Stevens song.

sentences.text: Good morning.
This seems like a good way to spend a Thursday.
This is our workday.
Somehow things are such that our work is here today.
Riding through our little city early in the morning on the way here, I always appreciate this sense that all of us are getting up and getting ready, trying to face our day, do our best.
So many people doing such important and essential work.
And that includes us.
Well, I don't think we're any more special, you know what I mean?
Any more important than anybody else doing this particular form of work.
Lots of people doing critical work today, including us.
Anyway, that often makes me think of this little Gary Snyder poem, which I probably read before, but it bears repeating.

I always figured Gary probably thought of this during sesshin while up in their place in the foothills of the Sierra, while the log trucks rumbled by, maybe after a moment of pride at this great thing to get up early and sit Zazen.
And then you realize other people have been up for hours, working away, doing important things.
So the title is "Why Log Truck Drivers Rise Earlier Than Students of Zen."
And the poem is:
*In the high seat before dawn dark, polished hubs gleam, and the shiny diesel stack warms and flutters up the Tyler Road grade to the logging on Poorman Creek, 30 miles of dust.
There is no other life.*
So there's no other life. 30 miles of dust, 30 minutes of breathing.
What's the difference?

So, as you may know, I set myself a Dharma Talk task this year to speak on all 48 of the koans, the Zen stories, in the Mumonkan koan collection, the best-known koan collection, at least in the Japanese tradition, called Gateless Barrier in English or Wu Ming Wan in Chinese.
But lately I haven't been giving any talks because it's been practice period.

During practice period we devote ourselves to Zazen, so there's less time in the schedule for talks, but also when there is a time for talks, we empower the Shuso to do the talking in conversation with us.

And hasn't that been great, with the talking also of the snow and the disruptions and so on, and there's still all the same talking about maturity, about meeting things as they arise, whether we like them or don't like them.
So I think this is a really important topic.
I'm glad we're thinking about it.
What is maturity, really?
Is there a thing called being mature?
Is there a state that somebody is a mature person?
Is it a trait, in other words?
And Scott, I appreciate the title he chose for the class, implying maybe so, but maybe more importantly it's a process, continuing our maturity, he suggested.
I thought it was really good.
Continuing our maturity, I like that it acknowledges that our inherent maturity is already here.
We start out with this natural human quality of maturity within us from the beginning.
But as he's pointing out, it doesn't happen by itself, it doesn't happen automatically.
Aging does not equal maturity.
It's something that needs to continue.
And maybe the way to think about it is we need to put ourselves into situations in which maturity arises.
Maybe the best thing is situations in which our only hope is maturity.
Nothing else will do, otherwise it's too hard.
So this involves some risk-taking, I think, and some mistake-making, and some embarrassment, screwing it up.
Whenever we try to learn about something, we always notice its opposite.
It's such a powerful pointer, so helpful.
It's so helpful to notice our non-maturity, too.
Not as discouraging evidence of our innate whatever, although we may think that way, but that's actually another pointer to maturity.
You look at the way non-maturity is pointing, whatever it may be, complaining, blaming, and you just turn around.
You just turn around and look the other way.
Now I know which way to go.
The opposite way.
And happily we don't have to become experts or figure this out.
We just listen to our suffering.
We feel how unpleasant it is to allow our non-maturity to run the show.
How constricting and unhelpful and demoralizing it is when we complain and resist our life the way it is.
But we don't actually really know how to do it.
Scott's giving us a lot of great tips, but I'm afraid they don't add up to much, because of the nature of the thing, that we don't really know what to do.
I like these lines from Wendell Berry that you've also heard before, I bet, called "The Real Work":
*It may be that when we no longer know what to do, we have come to our real work, and that when we no longer know which way to go, we've come to our real journey.
The mind that is not baffled is not employed.
The impeded stream is the one that sings.*
How do these poets do it, you know?
The impeded stream is the one that sings.
That's so brilliant, isn't it?
It's another way of turning around.
I feel impeded, this is annoying.
What's the opposite side?
Beautiful song.
Anyway, back to the Mumonkan.
Surprisingly, the next koan on my list, number five, is about maturity.

There's something weird about these Zen story collections, and I don't know if somehow they just magically are always the right one, or if they pretty much apply in all situations, and you can just talk about them however you want, and they're just really flexible, and probably a bit of both.
Case five of the Mumonkan is one of the dramatic stories that came early on to the West as Zen stories, before we really had that much context.
I was thinking they mostly arrived in the 1950s, but then in reading Robert Aitken's commentary on this case, he mentions a similar story in the volume *101 Zen Stories* by my hero, Nyogen Senzaki.
And just on a whim, I thought, well, that's probably completely unavailable and out of print.
I bet he typed it on a typewriter, and remember you grab five copies at the LA Library or something.
But on a whim, I looked on Amazon, and there were two options you could get of 101 Zen Stories.
One seems to be a facsimile of that typewritten copy.
You do the look-inside thing, and it shows you images, and there are corrections and typeovers, and it's like an old typewriter.
And the comments in Amazon complain about that: that's really hard to read.
It's a typewriter, for goodness' sake.
How could this be?
Then I was in a hurry, so I downloaded the Kindle version.
It was all computerized and nicely typed.
So now I have these old stories.
But the thing that surprised me, where I was going with that, was he published this in 1919.
It was a couple of years after he decided not to go back to Japan.
So it goes back a little while.
And anyway, he focused in that on interesting and dramatic stories that somehow bring forth, he felt, the spirit of Zen.
But I think the tradition doesn't find the exciting story koans any more or less important than the more enigmatic, simple exchanges between people.
Like, what is the real meaning of Zen?
Three pounds of flax in stock.
So that's also important, but the stories are fun.
So this one's a story.
*The priest Xiang Yan said, "It is as though you are up in a tree, hanging from a branch with your teeth.
Your hands and feet can't reach any branch.
Someone appears beneath the tree and asks, 'What is the meaning of Bodhidharma's coming from the West?' If you do not answer, you evade your responsibility.
If you do answer, you lose your life.
What do you do?"*
What do you do?
It's like a puzzle.
Another translator I looked up adds some more drama.
I don't know if this is in the Chinese or implied.
His version is:
*Zen master Xiang Yan said, "It's like a man up in a tree hanging from a branch by his teeth and his hands can't grasp anything and his feet are tied and bound."*
So even worse, you're tied up.
And then he says:
*"An emperor's general appears beneath the tree and asks, 'Why did Bodhidharma come to China?' If he does not answer, he evades his duty to respond to the question and he will be killed.
The general has a sword.
If he does answer, he will lose his life.
If you were that man in that tree, what would you do?"*
So in that version, we die either way.
A kind of conundrum.
And there are actually many more stories, many more trees too, but many more stories as well, of being up in a tree or hanging off a cliff or bouncing on a pole with nowhere to go, nowhere to go.
How do you practice when there's nowhere to go?
What do you do when you really don't know what to do?
It may be that when you no longer know what to do, you have come to your real work.
My favorite question to ask during the shuso ceremony, which we'll be doing on Sunday morning with our shuso here, is along those lines.
I sometimes find myself asking, "How do you practice when you don't know what to do?"
Which is of course an unanswerable question.
But it's a question that we can and should respond to, I think, when we receive it, whether we receive it in a ceremony or more likely when we receive it from our life.
And now I've tipped my hat, so I can't use that question, I guess, on Sunday.
Maybe I will anyway.

But also to let this serve as a little heads up, if you're not familiar with the ceremony on Sunday, there's a time for every one of us to bring something up, to ask a question, to make a statement from our heart about our dharma life practice.
And the shuso responds.
Which is a big part of the training of the shuso.
And also I think a wonderful example of the way the whole thing works.
It's not that we're testing the shuso or trying to see if he's going to do it right or something like that.
But the shuso generously puts him or herself in the middle like a mandala and we all participate.
Or like a bike wheel, puts himself or herself in the hub and we're all the spokes in the rim.
So we do it together.
It's a bringing up the dharma together that's empowered by this courageous person in the center.
But he doesn't know the answers, luckily, so he can relax.
He just does his best to respond.
Hanging from the tree as he'll be by his teeth.
And everything that we do here actually is kind of that way.
Dokusan, for instance, is the same idea.

It's not like the teacher, it's not like Andrea or I can see inside your head and then go look into our little storehouse of wisdom and pull out the perfect gem to give you and send you on your way with the perfect practice or something like this.
It's more like we do our best to set down these limited ideas of Tim or advice or getting it right.
And we just do our best to meet you fully as the Buddha that you are.
And something happens in that space.
In the Lotus Sutra it says the only way to understand this is when a Buddha and a Buddha understand it together.
So the shuso ceremony, dokusan, bowing to the servers, breathing, it's all like this.
It's a Buddha and a Buddha actually.
And we don't feel that way subjectively.
There's an important lesson there.
Which way should you turn when your thoughts are leading you into despair or judgment?
I was thinking as we were setting up the talk what a great setup this is for feeling judgment, isn't it?
You judge yourself: am I doing this right?
If you're the one sitting there, you judge somebody else: are they doing it right?
All these little details, are they being done properly and so forth?
So it's like a judgment-breeding factory.
Which helps us to see the mind that judges, right?
And the other way, and we glimpse the Buddha.
So anyway, the traditional commentaries of the story, at least the ones I looked at, and this book has the most commentaries, probably of all of them.
I know of about a dozen in English.
I got five or six of them.
And there are probably dozens and dozens in Japanese, and probably Chinese too, but the Japanese especially really love this book.
Japanese Zen people anyway.
So any of the stories about this man up in a tree, and really there's no reason for the figure to be gendered, actually.
This woman up the tree.
This non-binary person up the tree.
This all beings up the tree.
They tend towards the theme of the value of the impossible.
We're not really fond of the impossible.
We have a strong preference, I think, for the possible.
We're not really excited about not knowing.
We like to know things, and to be confident.
And I think we have the idea that all that kind of nasty judgment and stuff would finally calm down eventually if we did get it right.
Even though we know it won't work.
So there's a value here to facing the impossibility of not just the story, but of our life itself.
That everything is impossible.
And we have to respond.
We are called upon to respond.
There's also a lovely little message in this one about sacrifice: sacrificing ourselves, letting go, giving ourselves away completely to the Dharma.
Trying our best to do something useful in the half second before we hit the ground, something that will serve, something that will help.
Help others not just to get patched up, but help others to see what's facing the other way for them.
See their Buddha nature.
One of the well-known commentaries is by Yamada Kuan Roshi.
He was a Japanese Rinzai priest who was also a big part of the early serious practice, and not just reading about it but early practicing, sesshins with Robert Aitken and his comrades.
He describes a little back story.
A lot of the commentaries, the teachers have this great dodge that they do, actually.
They spend about half the talk telling you the biography of the teacher, and the biography of their teacher, and all the other interesting things that happened.
I so deeply appreciate Robert Aitken and met him once, and I've appreciated his students so much.
But he's really guilty of that in his book, actually.
He spends about five pages on all his back story, [unclear: "about a paragraph actually facing the story"].
So Yamada does that too.
And then he asks us a question, which is really the central question, isn't it?
He says, now you tell me, what would you do?
What would you do in this situation?
What should the man in the tree do?
Then he goes on with the classic Zen non-explanation.
He says:
*Every koan presents us with a problem that can't be solved.
It can't be solved by thought or reasoning.
The common sense of ordinary people rejects it as absurd. [unclear: "learning people, such as philosophers and scientists, for lack of reason in this koan.
Sense people"] are often perplexed when confronted by the strange and even abnormal expressions found in the language of the koan.
Koans bring us into a land of [unclear: "bounding"] and contradiction of ideas and concepts.
We cannot escape by means of rational thinking.
There's no other way of freeing ourselves from the confusion than by cutting through, as though cutting through a Gordian knot.
This cannot be done by rational thinking or logical reasoning.
It can only be accomplished factually.*
I bet you didn't expect that word: factually.
So then he goes on to explain "factually," from his point of view.
What is a fact in Zen?
*A fact is the manifestation of essential nature by an action, such as standing up, sitting down, eating, drinking, crying, or laughing.
In the case of Zhaozhou's Mu, Mu is a fact.
In the case of Gutei's finger, raising a finger is the fact.
One finger is Zen.*
In this case, the fact is some action of the man in the tree.

So I'm not sure in our lineage family we completely agree with the sort of anti-intellectualism there, but for sure a deeper approach is needed than just thinking it through or trying to figure it out.
There must be some response, some action.
I don't know why you use the English word "fact" for that, but it's kind of great.
The other night, Andrea was quoting her teacher Sojun, who quotes Suzuki Roshi, often I think, talking about finding our inmost request, our deepest response.
I love this other quote from Suzuki Roshi: the most important thing is to remember the most important thing.
How do we respond?
And how do we respond in an impossible situation?
The value of this quote for me is to really recognize, and keep remembering and reminding myself, that the whole thing is impossible.
Whether we're up in a tree or on our cushions or trying to talk to our kids or go to work or just be alive.
Being alive with a death sentence that we all have is sort of impossible.
Being alive in the age of climate change and global worry and destruction is impossible.
And yet we're called upon to respond.
To not respond would be going the wrong way.
So what is the Zen fact?
It's what your body, mind and heart can express and open through and with as you meet your life, as you meet the world, as you meet this moment.
And all of Buddhist epistemology and ethics reminds us that our actions really matter.
They ripple out through the universe in ways we could never fully know.
And our actions don't include just bodily actions; they include actions of body, speech, and mind, as I'm sure you remember.
So our thoughts matter too.
It's not like we can just sit here having nasty thoughts because nobody hears us.
Well, you could, but you'll suffer and it won't help, right?
You will lose your life in a way that's not so productive.
Maybe there's a Taoist infusion, like the stories of a butterfly flapping her wings and on the other side of the world a storm brews.
These stories are probably more true than we can quite imagine.
I also have a commentary by Nyogen Senzaki, and he has a totally different take on it, which is pretty interesting.
He says that Master Wu Men, Mu Man, the collector of the koan, left out a line, and he chides Master Wu Man for this.
Here's his version:
*A monk asked Master Xiang Yan, "Without using either relative or absolute terms, please tell me why Bodhidharma came to China from India."*
So this is before what we read.
A monk asked the teacher, without using either relative or absolute terms, please tell me why Bodhidharma came from China, came to China from India.
And then Xiang Yan replied:
*You are hanging from a tree by your teeth over a precipice.
Your hands can grasp no branch, your feet rest on no limb.
You must answer the question.
If you do not answer, you are a dismal student of Zen.
If you answer, you fall from the tree and lose your life.*
It's a little different timing here.
This whole tree story is a lesson for this monk asking this lofty, important question.
What is Zen?
What is Dharma?
What is life?
That's what's meant by these discussions of Bodhidharma.
You're putting yourself in that position, says Senzaki Hiroshi.
Should questions like this be answered?
And there's a wonderful tradition around restraint, as you might have noticed, right?
In sesshin we practice a lot of restraint.
Not talking.
I also recommend the restraint practice, the quiet, the silence practice, of not looking around.
Our mind gets a little bored, right?
We're desiring stimulation, so we look around.
Is Talus going to remember the next thing to bring in or not?
So maybe try not doing that.
Look down, close your eyes, let your gaze be low, just trusting that everything's going to work out.
Don't turn sesshin into a television show.
So there's a quality of restraint here, and Nyogen Senzaki goes on to say about his version of the koan, and this is really nice, I think:
*Why does this monk have to worry about Bodhidharma?
That blue-eyed Indian passed from the world a long time ago.
It does not matter whether Bodhidharma came from the west to the east or from the east to the west.
The concern in the moment for this monk is to realize Zen.
Best to even forget the term Zen, but to see his own true self the moment he acts.
If I serve you a cup of tea and say, "This is a symbol of Zen," none of you Zen students of our Sangha will enjoy such a lukewarm beverage.
But a stranger may come among us, and after sipping my tea, may express his appreciation.
Because he's a stranger, I will not say anything about it.
But if this were the case of an old-timer here, I would not allow such an unworthy comment.
Why?
Because sipping is the appreciation, and the appreciation is the sipping.
The thriftiest Zen student does not waste one-tenth of a word or the slightest movement of a thought.
Xiang Yan wanted to teach this monk the thrift of Zen.
And thus he stopped the use of his hands and feet and required the monk to be enlightened before he could open his mouth and fall from a tree into a precipice.
It's the same trick as cutting off the finger of the imitator in the third koan.
The kindness of such unkind action is to block off the road of thinking.
Zen would never say, "Try this method and you'll be enlightened."
It only demands that action which is already enlightenment itself.*
The kindness of such unkind action.
Great phrase.
Zen demands that action which is already enlightenment itself.
And he goes on:
*A good student always looks like a fool and never shows others her smartness.
The other's feelings are soothed and less harm is done that way.
Xiang Yan showed his foolishness and told the monk such a foolish story.
I admire his kindness.
Fools are born every minute.
Even in our time here in America we need this foolish koan.
Those who use this ego-killing medicine try to shut their mouths and cause tears to stream from their dead eyes.
What a pity.
Why don't you just open up your true eyes and laugh at the foolishness of both Xiang Yan and Mu Man, the collector of the koan.*
So it's good to be a little foolish.
Let's give ourselves more permission, as best we can, to not know what we're doing.
To let our inmost request, our inmost response, arise from wherever these things arise from, and express that action that's already enlightenment.
And of course we can't do this.
It's not the kind of thing that I do or you do, but the act of Zen that arises as we continue our maturity.
Lately I keep thinking again and again of what my teacher, our teacher Norman, suggested to me and my ordination littermates 20 years ago now.
He remembered this the other day, last year maybe, when he was here.
He was like, oh yeah, there's this thing I used to say, it's just been on the tip of my tongue all these years, when I'm in good shape anyway.
He said, the way to practice is: be humble, see everyone as Buddha, and try to help.
So sometimes this means opening your mouth.
Other times it means the restraint, keeping our mouths closed, letting things unfold without our meddling, trusting the situation in a certain way, responding more quietly.
Either way we're fools, and this is a glorious thing, even in a world that's burning.
So here's my little prayer for the morning.
May our joy and delight, our tears and our foolishness be a support to all beings, as we all face together the 10,000 joys and the 10,000 sorrows.
Each of us dangling from our own particular tree, our own particular version of the impossible situation called being a person.
That unfortunately is too bad for you, I'm the one talking.
And unfortunately it makes me think of the end of Life of Brian, which my son just watched for the first time.
So if you have that image in your hand there, there it is.
So, speaking of songs, let's close with a song.
I think a year ago here I sang a Cat Stevens song, and recently the Pickford has been playing classic cult films, do you see this?
They played Harold and Maud on the big screen, it was so great.
We went.
Everyone there was so happy, and it was a mix; it wasn't just people who remembered it from back in the day, there were young people who had never seen it too.
Great movie.
Anyway, Cat Stevens songs are the whole soundtrack.
I think it was like a Cat Stevens concert with a movie, a movie with a Cat Stevens concert.
And when I was looking up the lyrics of this particular song, cool Wikipedia fact for Harold and Maud fans: it turns out they first approached Elton John.
And Elton John said, no, no, no, it wouldn't be right for me, call up Cat Stevens.
So they did.
So thank you, Elton John.
Maybe there could have been an Elton John version, but it's hard to imagine.
Well, I think it's fine,
*building jumbo planes, or taking a ride on a cosmic train.
Switch on summer from a slot machine, get what you want, if you want, get what you want, if you want, 'cause you can get anything.
I know we've come a long way, we're changing day to day, tell me, where do the children play?*
*When you roll on roads, over fresh green grass, for your lorry loads, pumping petrol gas, and you make them long, and you make them tough, and you just go on and on, and it seems you can't get off.
I know we've come a long way, we're changing day to day, tell me, where do the children play?*
*Well, we've cracked the sky, scrapers fill the air, we keep on building higher, till there's no more room up there.
Will you make us laugh?
Will you make us cry?
Will you tell us when to live, will you tell us when to die?
I know we've come a long way, we're changing day to day, tell me, where do the children play?
Where do the children play?
Where do the children play?*
Indulging me there.
Continue hanging from our tree.
Trying to play.
Into every being.
